---
title: "Performance"
---

Every benchmark on this page is a **twin program**: the same algorithm written
twice, once in Jestyr and once in straightforward C or C++17, with identical
traversal order, identical checksums, and one hard rule — **both binaries must
print byte-identical output**. If the outputs differ by one byte, the pair is
disqualified. That rule is what makes the ratios trustworthy, including the bad
one at the bottom of the table. You are never comparing a program against a
subtly different program.

::: {.claim}
All benchmark pairs print byte-identical output, so every ratio compares the
same verified computation — including the parallel pair, whose Jestyr answer is
schedule-independent by construction and cross-checked against its own serial
pass in-program.
<span class="verify">$ cargo run --release -- run examples/cpp_compare/heavy_sieve.jtr</span>
:::

The sources live in [`examples/cpp_compare/`](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/tree/master/examples/cpp_compare)
alongside a README that states every caveat these tables inherit.

## Scope, first

Read the numbers with this frame or not at all:

- **One machine, one compiler.** Windows 11, gcc/g++ 8.3, `-O2`, medians of 7
  runs. Correctness is cross-platform — CI runs the full test ladder and the
  determinism canary on Ubuntu 24.04 with gcc 13.3 — but the *timings* are
  local. Measure on your machine before quoting them.
- **Single-digit percentages are code-layout noise.** They move between
  sessions, in both directions. The tables mark the ranges where we observed
  them.
- **The hot loops use Jestyr's raw-pointer idiom** (`unsafe` reads/writes over
  a flat buffer), matching what the C side does. The checked tiers — slice
  indexing with live bounds asserts, contracts, error unions — are a dial, not
  a mandate. Turn them on and you pay for exactly what they check; the
  `numeric_kernel` pair below runs *with* the checks on and still holds parity.

## Demonstration tier

Small programs, small enough to hold both versions in your head. The `fib`
pairs are twinned against hand-written C, `numeric_kernel` against C++17.

| pair | workload | jestyr speed vs twin |
|---|---|---|
| `fib(40)` | naive recursion, call overhead | 0.984× |
| `fib(45)` | same, deeper | 1.17–1.22× (layout noise, favoring Jestyr this session) |
| `numeric_kernel` | tight integer loops over two contiguous buffers, bounds checks **live** | ~1.0× |

`fib` swings past 1.0× not because Jestyr is faster than C — it emits C — but
because at this scale, code layout decides more than the source language does.
That is the honest reading of every single-digit delta on this page, in both
directions.

`numeric_kernel` deserves one asymmetry note: the Jestyr side is doing
strictly more work. `xs[i]` lowers to a bounds-checked access and the locked
flags do not include `-DNDEBUG`, so the checks are live at `-O2`. The compiler
elides them where the loop bound proves the index (the fill loop carries no
asserts in the emitted C) and keeps them where it cannot (the stencil's
`i - 1` / `i + 1` defeat the proof). Against idiomatic
`std::vector<int64_t>` the checked Jestyr build is at parity; against a
deliberately de-idiomized C++ variant (`new int64_t[n]`, no
value-initialization) C++ moves about 15% ahead. That 15% is the measured price
of live bounds checks on this kernel: not free, cheap enough that idiomatic
C++ does not beat them.

## Heavy tier

The `heavy_*` pairs keep the same twin discipline on workloads big enough for
timing to mean something.

| pair | workload | shape it stresses |
|---|---|---|
| `heavy_sieve` | Sieve of Eratosthenes to 50,000,000 (~50 MB of flags) | memory-bound, branchy, strided writes |
| `heavy_matmul` | naive 768×768 f64 multiply (~453M mul-adds), exact integer checksum | floating-point compute |
| `heavy_wordcount` | 10,000,000 LCG-drawn words into a hash map | allocation + hashing |
| `heavy_parsum` | parallel sum of squares over 20,000,000 i64 (~160 MB) | threaded reduction |

Medians of 7 runs, same machine and flags as above:

| pair | jestyr | c++ | jestyr speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `heavy_sieve` | 0.505 s | 0.458 s | 0.91× (0.9–1.2× across sessions) |
| `heavy_matmul` | 0.210 s | 0.202 s | 0.96× |
| `heavy_wordcount` | 0.274 s | 0.376 s | **1.37×** |
| `heavy_parsum` | 0.145 s | 0.087 s | **0.60×** |

::: {.claim}
Heavy-tier medians, one machine (Windows 11, gcc/g++ 8.3, `-O2`, medians of 7):
sieve 0.91×, matmul 0.96×, wordcount 1.37×, parsum 0.60× — all four pairs
byte-identical in output.
<span class="verify">$ cargo run --release -- build examples/cpp_compare/heavy_matmul.jtr</span>
:::

## Three findings

**1. Sequential code is at parity.** Sieve, matmul, and the serial halves of
every pair land within single digits of the C++ twin, with the deltas pointing
both ways across sessions. That is what you expect from a language that lowers
to C and hands `-O2` the final say: the deltas are code layout, not language
tax.

**2. Design decides the outliers — in both directions.** The wordcount win is
not a compiler trick. Jestyr's `std/strmap` is an open-addressing table with no
per-node allocation, written in Jestyr itself; `std::unordered_map` is
node-based because its ABI froze that way in 2011 and cannot change. A
standard library young enough to pick the right data structure beats a
standard library that is not allowed to — 1.37× on ten million insertions.

**3. The loss is named, scoped, and owned.** `heavy_parsum` is 0.60×: the
general `par for … reduce` lowering costs real overhead against hand-tuned
fixed-chunk `std::thread` code at this size. The serial halves of the same
pair match at parity, so this is lowering overhead, not a semantics cost, and
it is the compiler's named optimization target. What the Jestyr side buys for
that overhead is one line —

```{.rust}
var total = 0
par for x in xs reduce(sum) {
    total += x * x
}
```

— against a page of chunking, spawning, per-thread partials, and a join, plus
a guarantee the C++ version cannot state: the reduction is
declared-deterministic, so the answer cannot depend on the thread schedule,
and swapping the element type to one where `+` stops being associative is a
compile error instead of a silent wrong answer.

## The one-sentence claim

::: {.claim}
On these workloads, on this machine, Jestyr's checked-off hot-loop idiom runs
within noise of hand-written C and C++, wins where its standard library made a
better structural choice, and loses 1.7× on one parallel lowering it has not
optimized yet — with every comparison pinned by byte-identical output.
<span class="verify">$ g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -pthread -o parsum_cpp examples/cpp_compare/heavy_parsum.cpp && ./parsum_cpp</span>
:::

That is the claim in full. No geometric means over the table, no "up to"
framing. Two measurement notes if you rerun it: discard the first run of each
binary (a cold first touch of hundreds of MB dominates everything else), and
alternate which binary goes first, or the ordering silently decides the
winner.

## What this page does not claim

- Nothing here is cross-platform *timing* evidence. The determinism digest is
  verified on Windows/MinGW-gcc and Ubuntu 24.04/gcc 13.3 by CI on every push;
  macOS and clang are untested. Speed numbers are one machine.
- Nothing here compares against tuned SIMD kernels, BLAS, or a profiled C++
  hash map. The C++ twins are straightforward C++17, the way a working
  engineer writes it — that is the comparison a new language actually faces.
- Byte-identity of *emitted C* (the compiler's own guarantee) is a separate,
  stronger property scoped to the single-file and concatenated emission paths;
  see [Determinism](determinism.qmd). This page only needs the weaker,
  per-program form: twin outputs match.

Continue with the [Tour](tour.qmd) to see the language behind the numbers.
